newsitem.title: FRANCE: French shareholders escalate fight against CFF bid.
newsitem.headline: French shareholders escalate fight against CFF bid.

text.p: Disgruntled shareholders of Credit Foncier de France (CFF) have taken their battle against terms of a state-orchestrated takeover of the property lender to the courts in an important escalation of their fight.

Colette Neuville, head of the French shareholders' action lobby ADAM, said on Tuesday the group had asked Paris commercial court to order an independent evaluation of the worth of CFF, once France's second-largest bond issuer.
She said the group also had asked the court to overturn the slim 53 percent approval of the lender's 1995 accounts at last June's annual general meeting because of voting irregularities.

The bank, which has earned a mention in the annals of French banking horror stories after posting a 10.8 billion franc ($2.1 billion) loss last year, is slated to be taken over by state-owned bank CDC and wound down.
The shareholders' action group, some of whose members are nursing big losses on shares that once traded around 450 francs, is demanding that the CDC boost its 70 franc per share offer.
CFF's woes stemmed from a collapse of property prices and the end of its lucrative monopoly on low cost mortgages.

Neuville said the group's toughened stance was triggered by CFF's surprise announcement last Friday of a 402 million franc first-half profit, compared with a 12 million franc loss for the same year-earlier period, and its forecast of a "positive" full year result barring a fresh real estate downturn.
She said the half-year earnings statement showed that the 1995 provisions totalling 13.6 billion francs had been unnecessarily large.
"The (1995) accounts do not correspond to reality...they are a sort of fiction," Neuville said in an interview.
She also said that if the CBV stock market regulator gave a green light for the bid, the group would challenge the decision. The deadline for the CBV's decision was Tuesday.
She said the commercial court would rule on Thursday on its call for an independent assessment of CFF's worth and decide on September 19 on the demand to annul the 1995 accounts.

The government said in July that CFF would be taken over by state bank CDC and be the subject of a "managed wind-down". The move came after the lender failed to find anyone in the private sector to salvage it.

Until recently the bank, whose shares were suspended on August 28, had been widely expected to post a 1996 loss of 520 million francs. It attributed its change in fortunes to falling interest rates and a better than expected real estate risk climate. ($ = 5.090 French Francs)
